---
title: "Design Lab: A Real-Time Gaming Leaderboard"
---

# Design Lab: A Real-Time Gaming Leaderboard

Build a Go ranking API for a season of synthetic game results. Separate authoritative score events from the read-optimized ranking. The first design question is whether a result replaces a best score or adds points: these require different retry behavior.

## Contract and authority

Accept authenticated `POST /results` with event ID, player ID, season, and integer points. Store a unique result event before applying it. Only trusted game-result producers may submit scores. Provide top-N, player rank, and nearby-rank endpoints with bounded windows.

For the baseline, additive events update a database score transactionally with their dedupe marker. Replayed events produce no new points. Build a Redis sorted-set projection from the outbox; it can be rebuilt from durable score state.

The [Redis sorted-set documentation](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/sorted-sets/) covers ranking commands and member ordering. Define ties explicitly. For the first version use descending score, then the store's documented member order, and expose ordinal rank. Competition rank (“1, 1, 3”) is a different product contract.

## Go implementation boundary

Keep score processing and projection separate:

```go
type ScoreEvent struct {
	ID, Player, Season string
	Points             int64
}

type Scores interface {
	Apply(context.Context, ScoreEvent) (int64, error)
}
```

This is a domain sketch. Validate overflow and allowed score ranges before adding. If projecting into Redis scores, account for floating-point exactness limits; choose a bounded integer range representable exactly.

Avoid a blind `ZINCRBY` on replayed events. One option publishes absolute score plus a monotonically increasing player version, with an atomic compare-version-and-set in the projection. A delayed old update then cannot replace a newer score. Include the season in every key, event, and version comparison.

## Freshness and scaling

The API can return projection age or the last applied version so callers understand eventual visibility. An immediate read after a write may use the authoritative database until the projection catches up.

A single sorted set is a useful baseline, not unlimited capacity. Partitioned leaderboards make exact global rank harder: merging local top-N candidates can produce global top-N, but does not by itself answer every player's exact global rank. Describe that tradeoff before sharding.

## Acceptance evidence

Submit one result twice, deliver player versions out of order, tie three players, and switch seasons while old jobs remain queued. Assert deterministic ordering and no score leakage across seasons. Rebuild the projection from scratch and compare every score with the source database. Test overflow and an unauthorized producer.

Measure result-to-rank lag, top-N p99 latency, projection retries, and hot-player throughput. Add WebSocket rank updates only with bounded queues and reconnect snapshots; ranking correctness must not depend on a subscriber remaining connected.
